emergency.general: Call 190 for police, 192 for ambulance (SAMU), or 193 for fire. There is no single universal emergency number. Operators primarily speak Portuguese — if you don't speak Portuguese, ask hotel staff for help or use a translation app. In major tourist areas, some operators may understand basic English.

healthcare.summary: Complete health & medication guide for traveling to Brazil. Emergency numbers (192/190/193), pharmacy tips, yellow fever vaccination, restricted medications, and travel insurance advice.
healthcare.costForTourists: Brazil's public healthcare system (SUS) provides free treatment to everyone including tourists, but is often overwhelmed with long waits. Private hospitals in major cities charge $80-200 USD for consultations and offer much higher quality.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Comprehensive travel insurance is essential. Private healthcare is significantly better than public, and emergency evacuation coverage is recommended for travelers visiting remote areas like the Amazon.
healthcare.vaccinationsRecommended: Yellow fever vaccination is strongly recommended and may be required for entry from certain countries; it's essential if visiting the Amazon, Pantanal, or rural areas. Hepatitis A, typhoid, and routine vaccinations should be current.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro have world-class private hospitals like Hospital Albert Einstein and Copa D'Or. In rural and Amazonian areas, medical facilities are very limited and evacuation may be necessary for serious conditions.

medications.prescriptionRules: A Brazilian prescription is required for prescription medications. Foreign prescriptions are not accepted. Antibiotics and many other drugs are widely available OTC. Carry medications in original packaging with a doctor's note.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD stimulant medications (Adderall, Ritalin, Vyvanse)
restrictedMeds.note: Stimulants are controlled substances. Bring original prescription, doctor's letter, and carry only personal-use quantities. Declare to customs if carrying controlled substances.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is controlled. Some products may be available with prescription. Carry alternatives if possible.

restrictedMeds.name: Psychotropic medications (diazepam, alprazolam, etc.)
restrictedMeds.note: Benzodiazepines require documentation. Carry a doctor's letter explaining medical necessity.

restrictedMeds.name: Methylphenidate (Ritalin/Concerta)
restrictedMeds.note: Bring documentation and only the amount needed for your stay.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in Portuguese or English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry original prescriptions and a note explaining medical necessity. Portuguese translation of prescriptions is helpful.
medications.generalAdvice: Brazil's health surveillance agency (ANVISA) regulates medication imports. Travelers may bring personal-use quantities of medications in original packaging with a doctor's letter — Portuguese translation is recommended. Controlled substances require a prescription and doctor's note explaining medical necessity. Declare medications at customs to avoid issues.

controlledSubstances.note: Prescription required. Carry original packaging and a doctor's letter. Portuguese translation recommended.
Amphetamines including Adderall are banned in Brazil. No exemption for foreign prescriptions. Lisdexamfetamine (Vyvanse) is available locally but foreign supplies are prohibited.
Recreational cannabis is illegal. CBD products require ANVISA authorization. Do not bring cannabis or CBD products without prior approval.

connectivity.simOptions: Claro, Vivo, or TIM prepaid SIMs at airport counters or any 'loja' (shop). Need passport. Data plans are cheap — ~R$30-50 for 15GB.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at hotels, shopping malls, and many restaurants/cafes. Quality varies. Airport WiFi usually requires registration.
connectivity.bestOption: Claro prepaid SIM for widest 4G coverage. Buy at airport on arrival. eSIM via Airalo works well as alternative.

cultural.tipping: 10% service charge usually included in restaurant bills. If not, 10% is customary. Round up for taxis. Tip hotel porters R$5-10 per bag.
cultural.dressCode: Very casual, especially in beach cities. Beachwear only at the beach — wearing swimwear in town is frowned upon. Smart casual for nice restaurants.
cultural.greetings: Kiss on one cheek (Rio) or two cheeks (São Paulo) between men-women and women-women. Handshake between men. Very warm and physical culture.
taboos: The 'OK' hand gesture (considered vulgar in Brazil)
Rushing conversations — Brazilians value personal connection before business
Being excessively punctual (social events start 30-60 min late)
cultural.haggling: Common at markets, street vendors, and independent shops. Not at malls or chain stores. Be friendly and smile while negotiating.

safety.lgbtSafetyNote: Brazil has legal protections and a vibrant LGBT scene in major cities, but homophobic violence remains a serious concern, particularly outside São Paulo and Rio's tourist zones.
safety.naturalDisasters: Flooding and landslides occur during the rainy season (November–March), particularly in hillside favelas and the southern states. Droughts periodically affect the northeast region.
safety.pettyCrime: Petty crime is very common in major cities, including pickpocketing, phone snatching, and bag theft on beaches, public transport, and in tourist areas. Criminals on motorcycles frequently snatch phones and bags.
safety.violentCrime: Violent crime including armed robbery, carjacking, and mugging is a significant concern, particularly in favelas, urban peripheries, and at night. Brazil has one of the highest homicide rates in the world, though most violence is gang-related and concentrated in specific areas.
safety.soloFemaleSafetyNote: Solo female travelers should exercise heightened caution, especially at night and on beaches. Sexual harassment and assault do occur; stick to well-lit populated areas and use ride-hailing apps.
safety.notes: Brazil requires heightened awareness of personal security. Avoid displaying valuables, use hotel safes, and don't resist if robbed. Favelas should not be visited without a reputable local guide. Major tourist areas like Copacabana and Ipanema have increased police presence but crime still occurs.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: visa-free for 90 days (as of 2024). UK, EU, Australia, Canada also visa-free for 90 days.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: April-October (dry season for most regions). Rio: December-March for beaches but very crowded during Carnival. Amazon: June-November (lower water, better wildlife).

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 190)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (190) and ambulance (192) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the RIGHT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is recommended for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.

immediate: Move to higher ground immediately — do not wait for official order in rapidly rising water
Avoid all drainage channels, rivers, and low-lying areas during heavy rain
If driving, do not attempt to cross flooded roads — turn back
Stay away from hillsides that may be prone to landslides after heavy rain
after: Do not return to flood or landslide area until cleared by Defesa Civil
Avoid contact with floodwater — contamination risk (leptospirosis)
Monitor Alerta Rio (Rio) or CEMADEN alerts
